Routine blood tests generally cannot detect most cancers on their own; one source says that, aside from leukemia, “most cancers cannot be detected during routine blood work,” and other tests are almost always necessary [d1]. Another source adds that routine blood work may detect early signs of some cancers, especially blood cancers such as leukemia and lymphoma, but still says other tests are needed to confirm a diagnosis [d2].

The retrieved evidence also shows important limits: for NSCLC, a blood “liquid biopsy” cannot diagnose the cancer itself [d3], and in lymphoma surveillance, routine blood tests had limited value and detected only 5% of relapses in one study [d4] [d8]. Blood tests may sometimes provide clues such as elevated liver enzymes in metastasis, but results can still be normal even with advanced cancer [d5]. Specialized blood-draw screening tests exist, but they may miss cancer and require confirmatory evaluation, so they are not the same as routine blood tests alone [d6].
